text_blocks.snippet: Pathogens cause disease by invading the body and interfering with normal bodily functions. They achieve this through various mechanisms, including direct damage to cells, releasing toxins, and triggering excessive immune responses.
snippet_highlighted_words: by invading the body and interfering with normal bodily functions

list.title: Portals of Entry:
list.snippet: Pathogens gain entry through various routes, such as the skin, mucous membranes, or the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts.

list.title: Adherence and Colonization:
list.snippet: Once inside, pathogens often need to adhere to host cells to colonize and multiply. They use specialized structures like pili (fimbriae) for this purpose.

list.title: Invasion and Dissemination:
list.snippet: Some pathogens invade host tissues and spread to other parts of the body, potentially causing systemic infections.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. Damage to Host Cells and Tissues:

list.title: Direct Damage:
list.snippet: Pathogens can directly damage cells and tissues through toxins, enzymes, or by disrupting normal cellular processes.

list.title: Toxins:
list.snippet: Many pathogens produce toxins that can cause a range of effects, from mild discomfort to severe illness and even death.

list.title: Immune Response:
list.snippet: The body's immune response to pathogens can also cause damage. While the immune system is designed to protect, sometimes it can overreact, leading to inflammation and tissue damage.

list.title: Camouflage:
list.snippet: Some pathogens can disguise themselves to avoid detection by the immune system.

list.title: Suppression:
list.snippet: Others can suppress the immune response, making it easier for them to multiply and spread.
Pathways of Transmission: Pathogens must be transmitted from one host to another to persist. They do this through various means, such as:
Direct contact: Physical contact with an infected person or animal.
Indirect contact: Contact with contaminated surfaces or objects.
Vectors: Transmission through insects like mosquitoes or ticks.
Airborne transmission: Through respiratory droplets produced by coughing or sneezing.
Bloodborne transmission: Through blood or bodily fluids.

list.title: Bacteria:
list.snippet: Bacteria can cause disease by releasing toxins, such as those produced by Clostridium botulinum (botulism) or by damaging tissues directly, like Streptococcus species causing strep throat.

list.title: Viruses:
list.snippet: Viruses like the flu virus invade cells and hijack their machinery to replicate, causing cell damage and illness.

list.title: Fungi:
list.snippet: Fungi like Candida can cause infections like yeast infections, and some opportunistic fungi can cause serious illness in immunocompromised individuals.

list.title: Protozoa:
list.snippet: Protozoa like Plasmodium, the cause of malaria, can multiply in the bloodstream and cause fever, chills, and other symptoms.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, pathogens cause disease by disrupting normal bodily functions, damaging tissues, and triggering immune responses. Their ability to invade, multiply, and be transmitted to new hosts is crucial to their ability to cause illness.
